note: Every term here is one the examiner reports record candidates confusing or misusing (2020-2025), or one a confused term depends on. The sense is ours, written to match the syllabus wording. Use it exactly, everywhere.

terms.sense: The number of live births per 1000 people in a year.
The number of deaths per 1000 people in a year.
Birth rate minus death rate, per 1000 people per year; negative when deaths exceed births.
terms.homonym_warning: Migration is not part of it.

terms.sense: The number of immigrants minus the number of emigrants.
Moving into a country to live.
Leaving a country to live elsewhere.
Moving to live elsewhere within the same country, such as from a rural area to a city.
Moving to live in another country.
Something about the place of origin that makes people want to leave it.
Something about the destination that attracts people to it.
Too many people for the resources and technology of an area to support a good standard of living.
terms.homonym_warning: Not the same as a large population.

terms.sense: Too few people to use the resources of an area fully.
The make-up of a population by age groups and sex, shown on an age/sex pyramid.
People too young or too old to work, who rely on the economically active.
The number of dependants compared with the number of people of working age.
The number of people per square kilometre.
terms.homonym_warning: Not the number of people alone.

terms.sense: Where people live in an area and where they do not; the pattern of their spread.
Settlements ranked by size and by the number and order of their services, from hamlet to city.
The smallest number of people needed to keep a service in business.
The area served by a settlement or a service.
A service used rarely that needs a large threshold population, such as a hospital or a university.
terms.homonym_warning: Low-order services are used often and need few people, such as a food shop.

terms.sense: The land a settlement is built on and its physical features (water supply, flat land, defence).
The position of a settlement in relation to the area around it: routes, other settlements, the relief.
What a settlement does: its main economic and social activities (port, market town, resort).
The Central Business District: the commercial centre of a city, with offices, shops and high land values.
The zone at the edge of a city where urban and rural land uses meet.
The growth in the proportion of a country’s population living in urban areas.
terms.homonym_warning: Not the growth of one city.

terms.sense: The spread of a city’s built-up area into the countryside around it.
An area of self-built housing on land the residents do not own, often without services.
Countryside, with farmland and small settlements.
terms.homonym_warning: Not defined by a lack of development.

terms.sense: The point underground where an earthquake starts.
The point on the Earth’s surface directly above the focus.
The amount of energy an earthquake releases, measured on a scale.
A steep-sided composite cone built of layers of ash and sticky lava, found at destructive boundaries.
A wide, gently sloping volcano built of runny lava.
Where two plates move towards each other and one is subducted beneath the other.
Where two plates move apart and magma rises to form new crust.
Where two plates slide past each other; earthquakes but no volcanoes.
All the land whose rainfall drains into one river and the streams that join it.
The high land that separates one drainage basin from another.
A smaller river that joins a larger one.
A channel that splits off from a river and flows away from it, as in a delta.
The point where two rivers join.
The volume of water passing a point in a river each second (cubic metres per second).
Water soaking into the soil from the surface.
Water moving sideways through the soil towards a river.
The flat land beside a river that is covered by water when the river floods.
A raised bank along a river, built up by deposition during floods.
A bend in a river, eroded on the outside where water is fastest and built up on the inside where it is slowest.
A horseshoe-shaped lake left when a meander is cut off.
A landform of deposited sediment at a river mouth, crossed by distributaries.
Erosion by the force of water, and air trapped and compressed in cracks.
Erosion by rocks and pebbles carried by the water being thrown against the bed, banks or cliff.
Rocks carried by the water knocking together and becoming smaller and rounder.
Chemical erosion: rock such as limestone dissolved by water.
The movement of beach material along a coast by waves approaching at an angle.
A pillar of rock standing apart from the cliff, left when an arch collapses.
The low remains of an eroded stack, covered at high tide.
A long ridge of sand or shingle joined to the land at one end, built by longshore drift.
A flat rocky area at the foot of a cliff, left as the cliff retreats.
A white wooden box with louvred sides on legs, which keeps thermometers in the shade with air flowing freely.
An instrument that measures wind speed.
An instrument that shows wind direction: the direction the wind blows from.
An instrument that collects and measures rainfall, sunk into open ground.
The difference between the highest and lowest temperature in one day.
The difference between the mean temperature of the hottest and the coolest months.
A pointed leaf tip that lets heavy rain run off quickly.
terms.homonym_warning: It sheds water; it does not keep it.

terms.sense: The large-scale clearing of forest.
Extra warming caused by more greenhouse gases in the atmosphere from human activity, trapping more heat.
Jobs that extract raw materials: farming, fishing, mining, forestry.
Jobs that manufacture or process goods.
Jobs that provide services.
Jobs in research, information and development.
The share of workers in each sector of the economy.
Farming to feed the farmer’s family, with little or nothing sold.
Farming to sell the produce for profit.
Growing crops.
Keeping animals.
Farming with high inputs of labour or capital per hectare and high yields.
Farming with low inputs per hectare over a large area.
What goes into a farm or factory system: raw materials, labour, energy, capital.
What comes out of the system: products and waste.
A company that operates in more than one country.
The growing links between countries through trade, investment, communication and culture.
Coal, oil and natural gas, formed from ancient plant and animal remains.
terms.homonym_warning: Petrol is refined from oil; HEP is renewable.

terms.sense: Energy from sources that are not used up, such as wind, solar, HEP, geothermal, tidal and wave power.
Development that meets present needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
A statement that can be tested by collecting and analysing data.
A small trial of a survey to test its questions and method before the real survey.
Choosing a sample so that every person or point has an equal chance of being chosen.
Choosing every nth person or point, or points at regular intervals.
Sampling groups in proportion to their share of the whole population.
Data collected by the investigator.
Data collected by someone else, such as a census or a weather service.
Whether a method would give the same results if repeated.
The height and shape of the land surface.
An angle measured clockwise from grid north, in degrees.
A direction given as a point of the compass, such as north-north-east.
Eastings then northings, each with a third figure for the tenths across the square.
